en: The Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai says:
Seventh, [the Buddha-nature] universally constitutes the essence of all dharmas. The *Contemplation Sūtra* states: “Vairocana pervades all places.
Nothing exists outside the Four Noble Truths. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: “That which the Buddha has not...”
"The teachings are like the soil of the lands of the ten directions;
that which has been taught is like the soil on a fingernail. Kāśyapa said:
“Since these Four Truths have already been explained, those not yet explained should constitute five truths.
The Buddha said: “No.
It is simply that these Four Truths possess immeasurable aspects.”
If this is so, the broad opening constitutes four sets of the Four Noble Truths, as explained in detail in the section on the "Excellence of the Object.
One should know that suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are the worldly causes and effects of good and evil;
while the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*) are all supramundane causes and effects.
All take the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as their essence.
As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* says:
"From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established"—is this not what is meant?
However, as for the substance upon which they depend, its essence is wondrous and without distinction;
as for the phenomena that depend upon it, these phenomena possess both the coarse and the wondrous.
All phenomena exist in mutual dependence, and their distinctions can be known through discernment.
By examining these five flavors in detail, one can discern both the coarse and the subtle.
By opening up the coarse to reveal the subtle, they likewise become known, and so forth.
This concludes the brief explanation of the essence of the sūtra.
△ Third Major Section: Clarifying the Essential Principle (*zong*).

The essential principle is the throat and collar of practice and the vital path for manifesting the essence. It is like beams and pillars supporting a house, or the main ropes of a net; when the rope is pulled, the mesh moves, and when the beam is secure, the rafters remain.
The explanation of the tenet is fivefold:
first, distinguishing the essence of the tenet;
second, the formal elucidation of the tenet.
Third, the similarities and differences among various sutras;
fourth, clarifying the coarse and the subtle;
fifth, concluding with cause and effect.
Regarding the simplification of "principle" (zong) and "substance" (ti),
some say that principle is identical to substance and substance is identical to principle;
this is not accepted here.
Why is this? Since the fundamental principle consists of cause and effect, cause and effect constitute two entities; yet that which is neither cause nor effect is an entity that is non-dual.
If the entity were dual, it would not be an entity at all.
If the essence is non-dual, then the essence is not the thesis.
If the thesis is non-dual, then the thesis is not a thesis;
if the thesis were dual, then the thesis would not be the essence.
How can you say that the substance is the thesis and the thesis is the substance?

Furthermore, pillars and beams are the structural framework of a house, while the void of the house is what is occupied by those beams and pillars; one should not claim that the beams and pillars are the void of the house, nor that the void of the house is the beams and pillars.
If the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the essence (*svabhāva*) were one, the fault would be as follows.

Furthermore, if the thesis and the essence were different, then the two dharmas would exist in isolation: the thesis would not be a thesis that reveals the essence, and the essence would not be the essence belonging to the thesis.
The "tenet" (zong) is not a tenet that reveals the essence; if it were a tenet, it would be perverse and inverted, lacking the seal of truth.

The "essence" (ti) is not the essence of a school of tenets; if it were, its essence would be narrow and incomplete, and cause and effect would exist separately outside of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
If the essence of the school (*zongti*) were different [from its substance], the fault would be as described above.

Now, it is said that they are not different yet are different; this distinction between the school and its essence arises because one discusses cause and effect with reference to that which is neither cause nor effect. Thus, there is merely a distinction between the school and its essence.
The *Śāstra* states:
"If one departs from the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, it is all termed the work of Māra.
The *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra* states:
"The cause of the Mahāyāna is the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena;
the fruit of the Mahāyāna is likewise the true reality of all phenomena. This is its meaning.

One should know that the essence of the true mark (dharmatā) is pervasive and is neither cause nor effect; yet, when practice begins, one distinguishes the cause, and when practice ends, one discusses the fruit.

Furthermore, as for the distinction between the partial and the perfect, it is like the substance of bronze: it is neither beginning nor end. When it is intended to be cast into an image, it is called the "beginning of the image";
when its polishing and refinement are all complete, it is called the "end of the image."
This analogy refers to the perfect cause and effect.
If one considers the preparation of a vessel and its subsequent completion—the beginning and end of the vessel's existence—this serves as an analogy for the partial cause and effect.

To give rise to the mind of the seven stages of expedient means is called the partial cause; to realize the *sopadhiśeṣa* (with-remainder) and *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without-remainder) [nirvāṇas] is called the partial effect.
The opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is called the perfect cause; ultimate, wondrous enlightenment is called the perfect fruit.
If one understands this analogy, that they are neither identical nor separate, the meaning of our school's doctrine becomes clear.
For example, the true causal Buddha-nature is neither cause nor fruit; yet, that which is cause but not fruit is called Buddha-nature, while that which is fruit but not cause is called Great Nirvana.

Furthermore, the Buddha-nature is neither future nor original; yet it is said to be inherently present from the beginning, and that all sentient beings possess the very mark of nirvana, which cannot be extinguished again.

Again, it is said that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, yet in reality they do not yet possess the thirty-two marks; they shall obtain the adamantine body in the future. Because it is not future, it is called "original";
because it is not original, it is called "future."
The meaning of the "essence of the school" (zongti) is likewise so.
Master Yuan took the One Vehicle as his school, namely the Wondrous Dharma (*saddharma*).
He cites a passage, saying:
"This vehicle is subtle and wondrous, being unsurpassed.
I privately maintain that it is "one" in order to refute the "three"; however, by relying on the coarse rather than the subtle cause, it fails to encompass the beginning and the end.
Longshi said: "One simply takes the fruit as the primary principle.
The 'wondrous Dharma' is the essence of the Tathāgata’s numinous wisdom."

All that is coarse is exhausted in the subtle; movement and stillness regulate all things as the Dharma. Since the Dharma is both true and subtle, it is likened to the lotus flower; thus, the fruit-wisdom is established as the central tenet.
I maintain that a fruit does not exist in isolation; how then can its cause be discarded? Furthermore, this would contradict the text.
The Preface to the *Huiguan* states:
"The convergence of the three vehicles into one is the beginning of the vehicle."
"The perfection of wisdom and awakening is the zenith of this vehicle;
the dissolution of form and the clarification of the spirit is its culmination.
Master Kumārajīva sighed in admiration and said:
"If one has not deeply penetrated the treasury of the sūtras, how could one make such a statement?
Master Yin replied:

"The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is the wondrous realm of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). It takes the union of object and wisdom as its central tenet; because the object is free from the three kinds of falsity, it is called 'true reality.'"
Now, it is said that while the object [of the practice] is augmented, the fruit is omitted; thus, one's swelling will not lead to increased nourishment.
The Guangzhai school takes the cause and fruit of the One Vehicle as its central tenet: the preceding section constitutes the cause, and the subsequent section constitutes the fruit.
I maintain that both passages each possess their own causes and effects; if one were to exist while the other were omitted, it would contradict the scriptural text.
Some take the two wisdoms of the provisional and the ultimate as their primary tenet.
I say that in employing expedient means (*upāya*), one should clarify that these three are the core tenets of the sutra;
yet these three are what this present sutra rejects—how can you take what is rejected as its core tenet?
Furthermore, the Master said:

This is titled "The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma" (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*); thus, the title itself constitutes its central tenet (*mūla*). The "Wondrous Dharma" refers to the fundamental, true *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) attained by the Buddha. Because this nature is neither different from afflictions nor identical to them, it is called "wondrous"; thus, the tenet serves as the title.

This is the position employed by the masters of the Yogācāra school, who maintain that the eight consciousnesses constitute the ultimate fruit; however, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* now refutes this, asserting instead that they are the very root of saṃsāra.
A certain master says:
"The thesis is that [the Buddha-nature] is eternally abiding; however, this does not reach the ultimate, and thus it is an indirect expression (āvṛta-lakṣaṇa) clarifying its permanence.
I privately maintain that this is entirely contrary to the intent of the sūtra. If permanence were concealed, what would the thesis reveal?
"Being constantly unobscured, 'constant' (nitya) is not the primary tenet. A master says:
"This clarifies and elucidates the meaning of 'constant,' serving as a more detailed or abbreviated version of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*."
I say that those who take "permanence" as their tenet have no cause or effect regarding permanence, and thus permanence itself cannot serve as a tenet, and so forth. Others say:
"The myriad virtues are the tenet; provided one practices these virtues, all shall attain Buddhahood."
I say: if becoming a Buddha is the fruit, why not take that fruit as the thesis?
Others say: among the myriad virtues, one takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as the thesis.
I consider this view too narrow and furthermore conflates with the Lesser Nirvana. Some say:
if those who receive these various divergent teachings each derive benefit from them, then the various expositions cannot be deemed erroneous.
To hear without awakening, no teacher can be deemed right.
The intent of a single teacher is that awakening alone is what is valued; thus, awakening should be taken as the core principle of the sūtras.
As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says:
"If there were any fixed characteristic to the phenomena of birth and death, that would be the mark of Māra;
the Buddha-dharma has no fixed characteristic.
Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of what is not the Path as the Path, and speaks of the Path as not the Path; one should know that it is solely from awakening that this proceeds.
I say that if awakening is taken as the primary principle (*zong*), it is the realization of the fruit, not the practice of the cause.
To ask about the south while pointing toward the north is to confuse the cardinal directions.
Furthermore, if one definitively establishes awakening as the primary principle, this constitutes a fixed certainty; how then can it be called "indefinite"?
There are many such explanations, which cannot be cited in full here.

Second, as for the explicit clarification of the central tenet: from the beginning of the "Introductory Chapter" through to the end of the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices," this sutra refutes and discards expedient means to reveal the true Buddha-knowledge and vision; it also clarifies the actual cause and actual fruit of the disciples, as well as the provisional cause and provisional fruit of the Teacher’s gate.

Although the textual meaning is extensive, its essential points are summarized here as the actual cause for becoming a disciple; since the cause is primary and the fruit secondary, the preceding section clarifies the manifested cause and the manifested fruit.

From the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth" through the "Chapter on Exhortation," the origins are revealed and the fundamental nature made manifest; the provisional near-term lifespan is set aside to clarify the reality of the long-term ultimate fruit.

This also clarifies the true cause and true fruit of the disciple, as well as the provisional cause and provisional fruit of the master’s school; thereby manifesting the master’s true fruit. Since the true fruit is the primary cause and the [disciple’s] cause is secondary, the subsequent section clarifies the fundamental cause and fundamental fruit.
The preceding causes and effects together constitute the central theme of the sutra; this is its intended meaning.

Therefore, the sutra is divided into two parts—the main discourse and the sequel—and the treatise likewise comprises the fundamental doctrine and its traces. Both the Dharma and the parable are titled, and both the lotus and the flower are raised; the provisional and the ultimate aspects of both master and disciple are all contained therein.

Third, regarding the similarities and differences in cause and effect across various sutras: this refers to how the causes and effects of the traces (the phenomenal realm) may be either identical or different, whereas the causes and effects of the source (the fundamental reality) are eternally distinct from those of the traces.
As for cause and effect, they truly interpenetrate and seal all phenomena; what sutra, then, does not discuss cause and effect in relation to these?

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* clarifies that the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)—which is neither cause nor effect—is the essence; yet, by taking "only the cause" as its thesis, it employs the wisdom of *prajñā* to eliminate and dispel [all conceptualizations], which is precisely the intended meaning of "cause."
Therefore it is said:
"That which is called *prajñā* within the mind of a bodhisattva is called *sarvajñā* within the mind of a Buddha.
The text also states that because the bodhisattva possesses the cause of neither arising nor ceasing, they attain the fruit of *sarvajñā*, which is neither interrupted nor eternal.
Master Ryō’s preface states:
"The 'Chapter on Revealing the Profound' begins with non-abiding and concludes with non-attainment as it returns to the three types of wisdom.
Beginning and end are cause and effect.

The text also speaks of the "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*), the fruit of Buddhahood, as being established through the cause of *prajñā*; here, the cause is primary and the fruit is secondary.
Since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* proclaims the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and describes its cultivation over countless eons, one knows that this sūtra takes the cause as its central tenet.

The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* takes the two meanings of the causes and conditions for the Buddha-land as its central theme; in the *Ratnakūṭa*, Vimalakīrti asks exhaustively about both cause and effect, and the Buddha answers fully regarding both cause and effect.
Thus, we know that it employs both cause and effect together as its central theme.
Regarding the Perfect and Sudden teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*, there are differing views on its fundamental tenet (*zong*).

Some maintain that the cause is taken as the tenet, asserting that based on the title, "Flower Adornment" (*Huayan*) signifies the meaning of cultivating the causes through the adornment of myriad practices.
In this text, the characteristics of the forty stages (*bhūmi*) are frequently discussed; therefore, the cause is taken as the primary subject (*pakṣa*).

Furthermore, it is said that the fruit is the subject; according to the title, "Mahāvaipulya Buddha," "Buddha" is the name for the ultimate fruit, while "Avataṃsaka" refers to the myriad virtues of meditative concentration and wisdom that adorn the Buddha-body, rather than adorning the cause.
The text frequently discusses the matters of the *sāmbhogakāya* and *dharmakāya*, thereby taking the fruition (*phala*) as its primary tenet.

Furthermore, another interpretation states that it takes both cause and fruition together as its tenet; for instance, it says that the Buddha is the fruition and the *Avataṃsaka* is the cause. Since the text fully expounds upon the *dharmakāya* and also explains the various stages (*bhūmi*), it takes both cause and fruition as its tenet.
Because various sūtras differ in their specific conditions, their expressed tenets naturally diverge.
The *Prajñāpāramitā* universally addresses three types of individuals and focuses on the true cause and effect; in this respect, its meaning is distinct.

Regarding bodhisattvas specifically, there are further distinctions between those of sharp and dull faculties; the explanation for the causes provided for those of dull faculties differs from this principle.
However, as for the causes for those of sharp faculties, this principle remains the same.

In the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, the meaning of "Buddha-lands" encompasses both aspects; if one considers the causes and effects of the three kinds of Buddha-lands, their meanings differ, whereas if one considers the causes and effects of a single kind of Buddha-land, they are the same.
The *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra likewise distinguishes between those who are dull regarding the two conditions and those who are sharp, as previously analyzed.
Furthermore, by applying this principle across the causes and fruits of the five flavors, the analogy can be understood.
This constitutes the characteristics of the similarities and differences between the causes and effects of the various sūtras and those of the Trace Gate (jimen).

Second, regarding the fact that the causes and effects of the Fundamental Gate (honmon) are eternally distinct from those of the various sūtras: if one considers the real causes and effects of the initial practice of a *tri-piṭaka* bodhisattva, which lack provisional causes and effects, up to the point where it clarifies that the Buddha’s attainment of the Way under the Bodhi tree was not achieved long ago as a fundamental reality, these are not the distant origins of the Fundamental and the Trace.

The bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) also have causal practices at their inception; when discussing their fundamental and manifested traces (*benji*), it is in terms of supernatural powers and transformations, not in terms of fundamental and manifested traces from a remote antiquity.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (*Dapin*) states that bodhisattvas possess fundamental and manifested traces while the two vehicles do not, and it speaks of the Buddha attaining the fundamental and manifested traces of the dharma-body and birth-body at the beginning, but does not speak of them as being from a remote antiquity.

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* does not state that śrāvakas possess the relationship between the fundamental and the manifested; it merely clarifies that bodhisattvas abide in the fundamental and manifested aspects of the inconceivable.
While it speaks of the Buddha’s pure land, even what was seen by Śikhin was not something of long antiquity.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that Vairocana and Śākyamuni constitute the primary and the manifested; yet even Bodhisattvas have their own primary and manifested forms. If even Śrāvakas do not hear or understand this, how could they themselves possess primary and manifested forms?
Now this sutra reveals that the śrāvakas have a fundamental basis; that basis possesses cause and effect, which are shown as the cause and effect within the traces of the two vehicles.

It also reveals the traces of the Buddha: his birth from the womb in the royal palace is the birth of the physical body (nirmāṇakāya), and his birth at the tree of enlightenment is the birth of the dharma-body (dharmakāya); even the births of the two bodies during the intervening period are all merely traces.
One simply takes that which was first attained—the true and the responsive—and designates it as the "Root.
Therefore, the relationship between teacher and disciple, as well as cause and effect, in this Root is forever distinct from other sutras.

In the traces (*traces*) of the present sutra, the cause and effect of teacher and disciple share similarities with and differences from various other sutras; however, the cause and effect of teacher and disciple within the Root is something found in no other sutras. It is precisely this cause and effect that constitutes the wondrous core of this sutra.

Fourth, regarding the coarse and the subtle: if one takes the cause of the "half-syllables" (the conventional teachings) and the fruit of the Bodhi tree as the universal result, then this school [of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*] is considered coarse.
The causes and fruits common to the three vehicles explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, as well as these uncommon causes, are likewise so regarded.

Although it is said that a Bodhisattva practices Prajñā for a single day—like the sun illuminating the darkness—and that upon generating the aspiration for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), one immediately sports with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), this still retains coarse causes, such that the perfect cause cannot manifest alone.

Although it is said that the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) neither comes nor goes, this still retains coarse fruits, such that the perfect fruit cannot manifest alone; therefore, these are termed "coarse."

Although the Vaipulya sutras critique the causes and effects of the partial (ekayāna), just as lotuses do not grow on high plateaus or dry land, they do not distinguish how the partial may enter the perfect; thus, the perfection remains unmanifested, which is likewise considered coarse.
In the *Avataṃsaka*, when it first illuminates the lofty mountains, it speaks of the single perfect cause;
when it reaches the final body, it speaks of the single perfect fruit.
Furthermore, it carries along the distinct causes and fruits, and the points where these are carried are coarse.

Now, as the śrāvakas receive their predictions in this sutra, the doubts of the bodhisattvas are dispelled; they equally open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and together enter the single perfect cause. Revealing their origins to manifest their fundamental nature, they equally awaken to the true fruit. With the cause perfected and the fruit realized, it does not carry any provisional means and is forever distinct from other sutras; therefore, it is called "Wondrous."

Regarding "opening up the coarse": in the past, because their faculties were dull, they were not yet capable of hearing the praise of the causes and effects of the Buddha-vehicle. Therefore, by using the causes and effects of expedient means to draw them closer to their dispositions, and through the ripening of the five flavors, their minds gradually became open and serene. Thus, the coarse causes were resolved and transformed into identical wondrous causes;
all coarse fruits were resolved and transformed into identical wondrous fruits.
Therefore, those among the assembly who lower their heads and raise their hands to take refuge in the Dharma shall all attain the Buddha-way; there can be no cause other than the Buddha-way.
Once the Buddha-way has been accomplished, how could there still be a fruit that is not the Buddha?
Even the subtle causes of dispersed goodness are now all opened and resolved as entirely perfect causes; how much more so the practices of the two vehicles!
How much more so the practices of the bodhisattvas!
There is not one that is not a wondrous cause and effect.
V. Conclusion consists of two parts: first, the conclusion regarding cause and effect;
second, the analytical examination via four propositions.
Now, the sutras explain cause and effect precisely for the sake of leading those who practice the Dharma of birth into the Path.

If one reveals the provisional to manifest the real, it primarily causes those of the seven kinds of expedient means who have not yet entered the body of birth to enter; secondarily, it causes those who have already entered the two bodies of birth and dharma to advance further.

If one speaks of the vastness of the lifespan, it indirectly causes those whose bodies have not yet entered [the path] to enter, and directly causes those who have already entered the dharmas of birth to advance.
The "Chapter on Spiritual Powers" (*Ṛddhipāda-parivarta*) states:
"All the profound matters of the Tathāgata" refers to the profound principle, which is neither cause nor fruit; the causes and fruits are the profound matters.
From the seven kinds of expedient means, one first attains entry into perfection and ascends to the stage of the copper wheel; this is termed the cause.
Up until the point where only one more birth remains—if that single birth is transformed—one immediately attains wondrous enlightenment; this is termed the fruit.
From the second stage (*dvitīya-bhūmi*) up to perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), the intermediate period is termed both cause and causal-cause, as well as both fruit and fruitional-fruit.
To subdue a portion of ignorance by means of the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) is called the cause;
to sever a portion of ignorance by means of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is called the fruit.
Based on this liberation, one further cultivates non-obstruction; therefore, it is called the "cause of the cause.
From this non-obstruction, one further attains liberation; therefore, it is called the "fruit of the fruit."
Furthermore, the first ten abodes (bhūmi) serve as the cause, and the ten practices (caryā) serve as the fruit;
the ten practices serve as the cause, and dedication (pariṇāmanā) serves as the fruit;
the ten dedications serve as the cause, and the ten stages (bhūmi) serve as the fruit.
The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are the cause, and Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*) is the fruit;
Equal Enlightenment is the cause, and Sublime Enlightenment (*pratyakṣabodhi*) is the fruit.
Sublime Enlightenment is exclusively the fruit and exclusively liberation; it cannot be termed a cause nor can it be termed unimpeded (*anāvaraṇa*).
The first stage (prathamā bhūmi) is solely a cause and solely unobstructed; it cannot be called a fruit or liberation.
Why? Because in the first stage one perceives the Truth (satya), taking that Truth as the cause. That which precedes this stage is merely a semblance and is not the true cause.

If one takes inherent nature as the primary cause: the snapping of fingers and scattering of flowers are the seeds of the conditional cause; hearing even a single phrase is the seed of the revealing cause; and all who possess a mind are the seeds of the direct cause.
This refers to the seeds of the three causes of inherent nature as discussed from a remote perspective; it is not the actual manifestation, and therefore these are not taken as the [primary] causes.
Second, the analysis by way of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Question:
If it is said that entering the principle at the first stage is called the perfect cause and perfect fruit, how can the text state:
"By practicing and studying gradually, one attains the Buddha-way"?
Answer: One should provide a fourfold analytical classification (catuṣkoṭi) in two ways:
there is gradual perfection, there is perfect gradualness, there is gradual gradualness, and there is perfect perfection.

Regarding "gradual fulfillment": this refers to the seven kinds of expedient means outside of the ultimate principle, which together open up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; thus, one first perceives the perfect principle.

That one perceives the perfect principle is truly because, through the seven kinds of expedient means outside of the principle, one gradually enters the perfect cause; therefore, it is called "gradual fulfillment."
Regarding the phrase "gradually perfecting the three phrases," etc.:

"Perfecting gradually" means that upon first entering this Perfect [Teaching], one contemplates the three truths simultaneously and perceives the principle of the true aspect (dharmatā), wherein there is no difference between the beginning and the end. Nevertheless, regarding the practice within phenomena (*dharma*), one has not yet fully perfected it and must continue to study and cultivate; because this refers to the initial entry into the Perfect, it is called "perfecting gradually."
Advancing in superior practice is further termed "gradual.

This "gradual" refers to the progression from the second stage (*bhūmi*) up to equal enlightenment; this is the gradual approach of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*), not the gradual approach of those outside the principle.

Regarding "perfectly perfect" (*yuanyuan*): even at the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miaojue*), it is called "gradually perfect" and also called "perfectly perfect. The principle of perfection was already perfect from the outset; now, furthermore, the phenomena are also perfect. Therefore, it is called "perfectly perfect."

Furthermore, "perfecting the gradual" is like the first stage; "gradually perfecting" is from the second stage onward up to the thirty minds; "gradually perfecting" is from the first ground onward; and "perfectly perfecting" is the state of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*).

Although the thirty stages of mind (triṃśac-citta) equally possess the significance of being "worthy" (ārya), they are designated as "worthy" because they primarily involve subduing [afflictions] while only slightly severing them.
The ten stages (daśabhūmi) are designated as "sages" (ārya) because they primarily involve severing [afflictions] while only slightly subduing them.
Furthermore, the ten abodes are called "sages" (xian-sheng); the twenty minds are "holy sages" (sheng-xian); the ten stages and equal enlightenment are "sages" (sheng);
and wondrous enlightenment is the "sage of sages" (sheng-sheng). Now, borrowing the metaphor of the new moon: although its circumference is already full, its light and function are not yet complete;
this illustrates "perfect gradualism" (yuan-jian). From the second day to the fourteenth day, its brightness gradually increases; this illustrates "gradual gradualism" (jian-jian).
By the fifteenth day, this analogy becomes gradually complete, and thus it is an analogy of "the complete within the complete.
Now, although the moon has no actual waning or waxing, one distinguishes waning and waxing by means of the moon;
likewise, although the principle has no gradual completion, one judges gradual completion by means of the principle.
The fundamental tenet of this sutra brings immense benefit; it begins with the Perfect and Gradual teachings and culminates in the Perfect and Perfect.
It fully develops and perfects the causes and effects of the Mahāyāna, and so forth.
Question:
Since it is called both "perfectly gradual" (*yuánjiàn*) and "perfectly distinct" (*yuánbié*), should it also be so for the *Tōng* (Comprehensive) Piṭaka? Answer:
This meaning is derived from the *Sijiao zhang* (Treatise on the Four Teachings). What is its intent?
Regarding the Tripitaka, the Tripitaka is easily understood.
"Distinct" refers to the truths, objects, and perfections.
"Pervasive" refers to the ultimate truth.
"Perfect" refers to the realization of one beyond training.
"Universal" (tongtong) means being identical to non-arising.
The "Three Baskets" (Tripitaka) refer to the precepts, concentration, and wisdom within the Truth of the Path.

"Distinctive" refers to the distinction between the exhaustion or non-exhaustion of both fundamental afflictions and their habitual tendencies; it is the distinction between transforming others or not transforming others, and emerging into the conventional world or not emerging from it.
"Rounded" (yuan) means collectively realizing the truth.
"Distinctly" (bie bie) means distinguishing between the superior and the inferior.
The "Three Pitakas" (san zang) refer to the precepts, concentration, and wisdom cultivated within the immeasurable Truth of the Path (mārgasatya).
"Penetrating" means that all four gates accord with the center.
"Perfect" means the exhaustion of the five stages of dwelling.
"Perfect-perfect" means integration.
"Distinct" refers to the differences between the four gates.
"Comprehensive" refers to the mutual inclusion of the four gates.
"Treasury" refers to the perfect truth of the path, and the perfect precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
Since this meaning is thus universally applicable, it should also be gradually perfected; all four permutations of gradual perfection are thereby attained.
Once cause and effect are thus concluded, they are both established.
Thereafter, when distinguishing the coarse from the subtle and opening up the categories of the coarse and the subtle, everything is fully realized.

△ Chapter Four: Explaining the Function. This "function" refers to the wondrous capacity of the Tathāgata and the supreme utility of this sutra. The Tathāgata takes the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate as his wondrous capacity;

this sutra takes the severing of doubt and the engendering of faith as its supreme utility. It is precisely these two wisdoms that can sever doubt and engender faith; the engendering of faith and the severing of doubt arise from the two wisdoms. This is merely a matter of alternating discussion from the perspectives of the person and the dharma.
Previously, the principle was clarified by distinguishing it according to its essence, so that the essence of the principle would not be confused.
Now, the function is discussed by distinguishing it according to the function of the principle, so that the function of the principle will not be confused.
What is meant by this?
The thesis (zong) also has its function (yong), and the function also has its thesis.

The thesis-function is not the function-of-function; the function-of-function is not the thesis-function. The function-thesis is not the thesis-of-thesis; the thesis-of-thesis is not the function-thesis.

Regarding the application of the thesis (*mūla-prayoga*): cause and effect constitute the thesis, while the severing [of delusions] and the subduing [of afflictions] respectively constitute their applications.

Regarding the thesis of the application (*prayoga-mūla*): compassion constitutes the thesis of the application, while the severing of doubt and the engendering of faith constitute the application of the application.
If we discuss the fundamental tenets, let us set aside the matters of severing and subduing afflictions, and instead discuss cause and effect;
now, in clarifying their function, let us discuss only the severing of doubt and the generation of faith, while setting aside compassion for the moment.

If one grasps this meaning, then one will know that the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real can sever doubt and give rise to faith; this is the great function of the present sutra, and its significance is clear!
To discuss this function, it is divided into five parts:
first, elucidating the power and function.
Second, clarifying similarities and differences;
third, clarifying the specific categories;
fourth, correlating with the four *siddhāntas*.
V. Concordance and Differences in *Siddhānta*. 1. Clarifying the Application:

The various sutras do not exclusively clarify the Buddha; thus, his wisdom does not fully manifest. The Buddha himself appears as a provisional trace (*saṃvṛti-nirmāṇa*), not primarily to refute and abolish the fruits of the Two Vehicles, nor to sever the immediate doubts of Bodhisattvas in their birth-bodies (*janma-kāya*). Rather, he arouses distant faith and does not reveal the original ground (*mūla-bhūmi*). This increases the path of great mindfulness of the Buddha for Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and diminishes [attachment to] births outside the realms (*dhātu*).
Such functional power as this is not found in other sutras; this present sutra possesses it in its entirety, which is why it is titled with this chapter.
It does not discuss the wisdom of the two vehicles or bodhisattvas, but exclusively reveals the subtle and wondrous wisdom of the Buddha;
it does not open up the knowledge and vision of the nine dharma-realms of sentient beings, but exclusively opens up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision for sentient beings.
Other sutras merely state that what is manifested by the Buddha is a trace, but do not state that the Buddha’s own body is itself a trace;
this present sutra, however, explicitly states that the Buddha’s own body is a trace—how then could his other manifestations not also be traces?
Now this sutra specifically refutes and discards the fruits of the two vehicles—the City of Transformation; how much more so their causal practices!

Furthermore, it refutes the attachment of Bodhisattvas who have received the provisional teachings and take those traces as ultimate; now all such attachments are discarded and revealed to be merely expedient traces. All intermediate doubts are completely severed, giving rise to profound, far-reaching, and inconceivable faith.
Furthermore, it reveals the true merits of the fundamental stage, enabling the Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body to attain great benefit.
Beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the final *ḥ* (visarga),
even if one were to grind as many lands in the ten directions as there are *nayutas* of dust particles to increase the number of Bodhisattvas on the path, one could not exhaust them.

This is because the Tathāgata rains the single-flavored rain of the two wisdoms—the provisional and the real—falling equally upon all four directions; this signifies that all four gates are simultaneously shattered.
For those who seek fulfillment through the Path of Perfection, he severs their deep doubts, arouses great faith, and causes them to enter the single, perfect cause.

Mounted upon the Mahāyāna chariot, they travel through the four quarters until reaching the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); yet even with such great function and great power, such wondrous capability and wondrous benefit, they are still not yet exhausted.
Furthermore, this power can shatter the fruits of the two vehicles.

Those of the two vehicles fear birth and death; they enter into emptiness to attain realization, giving rise to the notion of security and the notion that they have already crossed over, thereby falling into the pit of the three unconditioned states.

Whether it be death or the suffering equivalent to death, once [the seeds of affliction] have become like withered seeds that will never sprout again, the wise physician folds his hands in impotence, and prescriptions and medicines are of no use.
As for the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* being able to cure even the icchantikas, this is considered easy.
The mental faculty of an icchantika is not extinguished; for all who possess a mind shall eventually attain Buddhahood. They are not those destined for death, and their cure is not difficult.

As for the Two Vehicles, they "ash their bodies and extinguish their wisdom": ashing the body means that form is no longer permanent, and extinguishing wisdom means that mental deliberation has already ceased.

Like scorched sprouts and ruined seeds, they further dwell upon high plateaus and dry land; being both deaf and mute, they shall never again turn back, abandoned by all the Teachers and for whom the medicines of the various sutras are of no avail.

Now, the Buddha-wisdom is fundamental and great, and the medicine of the wondrous Dharma is excellent; the physical body does not turn to ash but is like pure lapis lazuli, wherein all internal and external forms and images appear. This causes the mind-intelligence not to perish, opening, revealing, awakening, and leading others into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
They cause lowly laborers to inherit the family estate of Bodhi; they bestow upon the high plains and dry lands the lotus flowers of the Buddha.
Their ears simultaneously hear the sounds of the ten dharma realms;
their tongues, according to all types of beings, proclaim the voice of the Buddha so that all may hear it.
To be able to employ a single faculty universally for all purposes is precisely the power and function of this present sutra.
Having already explained the Buddha’s power of wisdom above, it is now stated once more.

For instance, during the Three Kingdoms period at the end of the Han dynasty, although Cao Cao’s strategic brilliance was first in the world at that time, he was still inferior to Yang Xiu by thirty-five *li*.

This is because the wisdom of people within the land of China does not equal the wisdom of those outside the realm, such as the non-Buddhist practitioners; it is like comparing a mustard seed to a mountain.
The wisdom of all worldly people and non-Buddhists does not equal even one-sixteenth part of Śāriputra’s wisdom.
The wisdom of the two vehicles is like the light of a firefly, while the wisdom of a bodhisattva is like the light of the sun.
The wisdom of the bodhisattva of general penetration is like a wild goose or a crane; its momentum does not reach far.
The wisdom of the bodhisattva of specific penetration is like a golden-winged garuḍa; it travels from one Mount Sumeru to another.
The wisdom of other bodhisattvas is like the soil on a fingernail, while the Buddha’s wisdom is like the soil of the ten directions.

One should know that the Buddha’s wisdom is supremely harmonious, supremely immediate, supremely sudden, and supremely real; it is inconceivable, neither vertical nor horizontal, perfectly wondrous and beyond compare, such that no analogy can exhaust its description through question and answer.
Other sutras do not explain this exclusively; only this present sutra explains it purely. This demonstrates the greatness of the Buddha’s true power of wisdom.

For example, ten young oxen, or even ten dragons, ten *nāgas*, one strongman, or ten strongmen, are not equal to a person with the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*). Those with external fivefold powers are not equal to a single *arhat*. All *arhats* are not equal to one Maudgalyāyana. Maudgalyāyana is not equal to Śāriputra. Śāriputra is not equal to a Bodhisattva. A Bodhisattva is not equal to another Bodhisattva. Another Bodhisattva is not equal to a Perfect Bodhisattva (*pariniṣpanna-bodhisattva*). A Perfect Bodhisattva is not equal to the Buddha.

The Buddha’s traces are exceedingly vast; he transforms and further creates transformations, and these transformations are inexhaustible. Without deliberation, he acts with perfect appropriateness, like the lute of the asuras; among all worthies and sages, none are able to fathom him.
Since the power of the Buddha is thus, other analogous points may be understood accordingly and need not be recorded further.
Second, explaining the similarities and differences.
Question:

Regarding the essence of the true mark (*dharmatā*) and the principle of cause and effect, since these are already common to all sutras, how do the two types of wisdom—the provisional and the ultimate—differ?
Answer: Although their names are used interchangeably, their functional power (*bala*) is vastly different.
In the *Zang* (Āgama) and *Tong* (Vaipulya) teachings, one uses the two types of wisdom to sever the doubts of the four abidings and give rise to faith in the partial truth (*prādeśika-satya*).

Although the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* rebukes the followers of the Two Vehicles and bodhisattvas of partial practice, it likewise involves severing doubts and giving rise to faith within the realm of the conditioned; it cannot cause those of the Small Vehicle or bodhisattvas of expedient means to sever great doubts and give rise to great faith.

The general meaning of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is that within the realm [of desire], doubt is severed and faith arises; although its specific meaning pertains to being outside the realm, it likewise involves the severing of proximate doubt and the arising of remote faith.

The primary intent of the *Avataṃsaka* is to sever doubts regarding that which lies beyond the realms and to give rise to perfect faith; yet it does not sever [the distinction between] the near and the far.
Therefore, although the two designations "provisional" (*prajñapti*) and "real" (*bhūta*) are used interchangeably, their functional power differs greatly.
Now, this sutra employs the two wisdoms of the Buddha’s bodhi to sever the seven kinds of greatest ignorance of expedient means, thereby entering together into the perfect cause.

It shatters the attachments to recent traces, giving rise to profound faith in the original ground; furthermore, even up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment, it causes one to sever doubt and give rise to faith.
How could such supreme efficacy be the same as that found in other scriptures?

Now, speaking specifically, it "destroys three to reveal one," which means it primarily destroys the three deluded attachments and reveals the single wisdom.

Why is this? If, in the past, I had first praised the Buddha-vehicle while sentient beings were submerged in suffering, they would not have been able to hear the Great [Vehicle]. Therefore, recollecting the power of the skillful means practiced by the Buddhas of the past, I likewise ought to teach the three vehicles.

Having already taught the three vehicles, [the Buddha] accommodated the teachings to the three types of deluded attachments, so that those who were not yet inclined toward the superior [truth] would not be discouraged.
Now, in order to shatter these three attachments and reveal the Buddha’s wisdom, it is said: "After a long time, the Buddhas must speak the ultimate truth."
Regarding "abolishing three to manifest one," this refers specifically to the abolition of the teachings.

Although their emotional attachments may be destroyed, if the teachings are not abolished, the conceptualizations they have established will arise again; by clinging to the teachings, delusions are produced. For this reason, the teachings are abolished.
Directly abandoning expedient means, he teaches only the Unsurpassed Way; throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma, neither two nor three.
Regarding "opening the three to reveal the one": this primarily concerns the principle (*li*), while incidentally it may be applied to the teachings (*jiao*).

As for the application to the teachings: the former teachings clarify that the three types of persons enter into truth (*zhen*); the present teaching clarifies that the three types of persons attain Buddhahood.
Regarding the correct principle, it is simply that the emptiness of the Two Vehicles inherently possesses the true mark (*dharmatā*).
In the past, because their skillful means were not profound, they were unable to see this wondrously.
Now, this emptiness is revealed to be the true mark; therefore, it is said that the definitive understanding of the Śrāvaka teachings is the king of all sutras.
He opens the gate of expedient means and reveals the true reality.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"For the sake of all śrāvakas, he develops their eye of wisdom."
Regarding the convergence of the three vehicles to reveal the One Vehicle, this refers precisely to practice.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states in its essential teaching:
"The four foundations of mindfulness, the four dhyānas, and so forth, are all the Mahāyāna."
"However, they had only realized the Dharma, but not yet realized the person.
This sutra brings both the person and the practice together; therefore it says:

'The path you are practicing is the Bodhisattva path; by gradually training and studying, you shall all become Buddhas,' and so forth, including such statements as 'lowering the head or raising the hand, all shall attain the Buddha-way.'"

Regarding "abiding in one and manifesting one": this refers to the Buddha’s original intent. Originally, he transforms sentient beings through true wisdom; the Buddha teaches with impartiality, like rain of a single flavor. The Buddha himself abides in the Great Vehicle, and according to the Dharma he has attained—adorned by the power of concentration and wisdom—he delivers sentient beings thereby.
If I were to transform others through the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), I would fall into stinginess and greed; such a thing is not permissible.
Therefore, know that from the night I attained the Way, I have always preached the Middle Way and always preached the Mahāyāna.

Yet, because of the transgressions of sentient beings, the Tathāgata smeared poison upon milk, donned tattered and filthy robes, and employed skillful means (*upāya*) and harmony to lead them toward the Great [Vehicle].
Therefore, it is said that although various paths are taught, in reality they constitute a single vehicle (*ekayāna*), and so forth.
Regarding "abiding in three to manifest one": this refers to the Buddha’s provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) as he employs skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to transform sentient beings.
Recalling the power of skillful means practiced by the Buddhas of the past, I now do likewise; I shall proceed to Vārāṇasī and, by means of skillful means, preach for the sake of the five bhikṣus.

The Buddhas of the past likewise dwelt within the Three Vehicles to manifest the One Vehicle; the present Buddha does the same. Therefore, it is said: "Furthermore, by means of various skillful expedients, he assists in manifesting the ultimate truth."
Furthermore, although in the past he disparaged the śrāvakas before the Bodhisattva, the Buddha was in fact liberated by means of the Mahāyāna.
As for "abiding in that which is neither three nor one to manifest the One," this may be understood either in terms of principle (*li*) or in terms of phenomena (*shi*).

Regarding the principle: this is the abiding of phenomena in their own positions; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. This dharma cannot be shown; know that dharmas are eternally without self-nature, for the seeds of the Buddha arise from conditions.
The absence of intrinsic nature is neither three nor one; arising from conditions means that the three conditions manifest as one, thereby causing one to realize that which is neither three nor one.
In terms of phenomena, this refers to the vehicles of humans and devas; these vehicles are neither three, nor are they one.

I constantly lead others into the Great Vehicle by means of this vehicle; whether they bow their heads or raise their hands, all shall attain the Buddha-way. Whenever I encounter sentient beings, I teach them all the Buddha-way.

Regarding "concealing three and revealing one": this refers to the manifold skillful means of the Buddha. In his prior provisional teachings and prior deliverances, he merely removed the disease without removing the medicine; because the medicine was not to be discarded, it was intended to transform future conditions. If this dharma were destroyed, what would there be for later use?
When the occasion ceases, it is concealed; when the occasion arises, it is employed. This applies not only to the Buddha, but likewise to bodhisattvas who have entered the reality.
If there are those who do not believe this teaching, one should, regarding other profound teachings, instruct, benefit, and gladden them, and so forth.

Regarding "abiding in three while employing one": this refers to the wondrous response-body and its retinue within the Dharma-body. The previous "abiding in three" to manifest "one" pertains to the teacher’s gate; the present "abiding in three while employing one" pertains to the disciple’s gate.

Pūrṇa and others like him are in truth the Dharmakāya; they manifest as śrāvakas, demonstrating abiding in the three vehicles while constantly revealing the One, thereby benefiting their fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring.

Regarding "abiding in one [vehicle] while employing three": this refers to his original vow. For example, when Puṣyarṇa became a Buddha, he vowed to preach the Three Vehicles, yet it was not in an evil age.
Now, this Buddha likewise made a vow before Ratnagarbha Buddha to preach these Three Vehicles in an evil age, and so forth.

However, the great function of the provisional and the real encompasses the entire Dharma-realm; how could it be limited to these ten points alone? It is merely to manifest the function of the Ten Subtleties that these ten are briefly mentioned.

Breaking the three to reveal the one is the excellence of wisdom; abolishing the three to reveal the one is the excellence of preaching the Dharma; opening the three to reveal the one is the excellence of the object; unifying the three to reveal the one is the excellence of practice; abiding in the one to reveal the one is the excellence of the vehicle; abiding in the three to reveal the one is the excellence of response and resonance; abiding in that which is neither three nor one to reveal the one is the excellence of supernatural powers; concealing the three to reveal the one is the excellence of stages; abiding in the three while employing the one is the excellence of the retinue; and abiding in the one while employing the three is the excellence of benefit.
By correlating the ten functions with the ten subtleties and distinguishing between their textual expressions and meanings, the general purport can be understood as follows.

To abide in the fundamental while employing the trace means that although one is immovable in the fundamental ground, the trace pervades the Dharma-realm; it is not born, yet manifests birth; it is not extinguished, yet manifests extinction. One constantly employs this trace to benefit and bring profit to sentient beings.
This meaning is based on the Master.

If based on the disciples, they are the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas, who abide in their original ground by means of non-abiding dharmas; through their effortless skillful means, their manifested functions are inexhaustible.
The text says:
"Furthermore, son of good family!
For all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, the Dharma is thus; for the sake of delivering sentient beings, it is entirely real and not false."

The Buddha’s responses were directed toward various conditions, and the text is slightly disordered; I have now titled this section "Citing the Text to Verify the Meaning" and conclude it by quoting from the "Life Span" chapter.
To shatter the traces and reveal the fundamental, and to harmonize the traces to reveal the fundamental, the distinct application of the cause is subtle.
"Revealing the trace to manifest the fundamental" refers, in its distinct discourse, to the excellence of the fundamental fruit.
"Abiding in the fundamental to manifest the fundamental" refers, in its distinct function, to the excellence of the fundamental land.
"Discarding the trace to manifest the fundamental" refers, in its distinct discourse, to the excellence of the fundamental teaching.
Abiding in that which is neither the trace nor the fundamental, the distinct teaching concerns the wondrousness of the fundamental in its responsive resonance (*ganying*).
Concealing the trace to manifest the fundamental, the distinct teaching concerns the wondrousness of the fundamental in its supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Abiding in the trace while employing the fundamental, the distinct teaching concerns the wondrousness of the fundamental in its lifespan, as well as the wondrousness of the fundamental in its retinue.

Abiding in the fundamental while employing the derivative, when discussed separately, this "employment" is the fundamental wondrousness of *nirvāṇa*, which is also the wondrousness of fundamental benefit, and so forth.

Fourth, regarding the conclusion that establishes the *siddhāntas*: the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real have ten different modes of application; these constitute the single voice of preaching, wherein each type of being understands according to its own kind.
The dismantling within the traces causes the seven kinds of skillful means to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

the dismantling within the fundamental reality causes the bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to sever their doubts and increase their path—both are the intent of the four *siddhāntas*, maturing sentient beings.
Now, these ten applications are condensed into the four *siddhāntas*:
first, condensing the provisional gate;
second, condensing the fundamental gate.
The traces are further divided into two:
first, the specific summary;
second, the general summary.

As for the distinctions: "opening the three to reveal the one," "abiding in the three while employing the one," and "converging the three to return to the one"—these three principles belong to the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint established for the benefit of individuals). Why is this so?

Having originally practiced these three, one now returns to cultivating the One by means of the three; thus, one does not alter the path or change the tracks, but simply deepens the contemplation of these three, and the single principle manifests of itself.

Since the One is contained within the three, there is no need for selection or rejection; therefore, opening up the three to manifest the one belongs to the *puruṣapudgala-siddhānta* (the teaching tailored to individuals).

Abiding in three while employing one is likewise: it is simply by relying on these three that one cultivates the single path. For example, Pūrṇa abided solely as a śrāvaka to benefit himself, yet he was also able to benefit his fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life; this is precisely not altering the three dharmas while being able to give rise to a single understanding—all of which belongs to the *puruṣakāra-siddhānta* (the standpoint for the benefit of others).
The three "shattering," the three "abolishing," and the three "concealing" belong to the category of counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*).

Among these, the three "sealing" and the one "doubting" serve to refute their emotional attachments, abolish provisional teachings, and secretly conceal provisional dharmas; this causes them to abandon their diseased minds and enter the single path of ultimate reality, abiding therein in the wisdom of reality (*bhūta-jñāna*).
Abiding in three to manifest one, and abiding in one while employing three—these two modes belong to the *loka-siddhānta* (the worldly standpoint). Why?

Because the world takes desire as its basis; if sentient beings wish to attain the path of the Three Vehicles and do not wish to hear the teaching of the single reality, the Buddha himself abides in the One and speaks of the Three in accordance with them.
Furthermore, because the objects of the three vehicles differ—just as worlds are distinct—they are called the world-standpoint (loka-siddhānta).
To abide in the three [vehicles] while manifesting the one is likewise the world-standpoint.

Why is this? The Buddha accords with the capacities of beings and abides in skillful means (*upāya*); he matures them and reveals the One, and thus this belongs to the world-standpoint (*loka-siddhānta*).
To abide in the One and reveal the One, or to abide in that which is neither three nor one and reveal the One—this belongs to the ultimate standpoint (*paramārtha-siddhānta*).
To thoroughly understand the four *siddhāntas* is simply to destroy the three [vehicles] to reveal the One, thereby attaining four kinds of benefit.

Why is this? A gentleman delights in hearing his own faults, while a petty person loathes hearing of their transgressions; yet, one who wishes to know their faults must surely reform them. This constitutes the destruction of attachments and the removal of maladies. To joyfully practice accordingly is precisely the worldly (*loka*) standpoint.

If one clings to the three [stages], one cannot advance on the Path; by breaking through the three and following the one, the mind of awakening arises and wholesome dharmas increase—this is what is called a "person."
To hold that three are a disease and to declare that one is bliss is called "counteractive treatment" (pratipakṣa).
If, upon hearing the refutation of the three, one attains insight into the principle, this is called the "ultimate truth" (paramārtha).
The other nine types follow this same pattern.

Thus, one should know that the Buddha’s skillful means accord with the capacities and conditions of sentient beings, causing all to obtain benefit; this is due to the power of the four *siddhāntas*, and so forth.
Second, regarding the conclusion of the section on the ten functions of the fundamental gate as the four *siddhāntas*, there are both specific and general meanings.

Abiding in the traces to manifest the fundamental, and abiding in the fundamental to employ the traces, belongs to the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint), also termed "according to desire"; the explanation is as before.

"Revealing the trace to manifest the fundamental," "converging the trace to manifest the fundamental," and "abiding in the function of the trace through the fundamental" belong to the *puruṣapudgala-siddhānta* (the standpoint for the benefit of persons). This does not involve altering the path to practice anew; rather, it involves practicing and manifesting the fundamental by returning to the original dharma. The explanation is as before.
"Destroying the traces," "abolishing the traces," and "covering the traces" belong to the category of remedial means (*pratipakṣa*).

"Abiding in the fundamental to manifest the fundamental" and "abiding in that which is neither fundamental nor a trace to manifest the fundamental" belong to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); their explanation is as previously stated.
Next, summarizing this section as a whole, the four *siddhāntas* are concluded as previously described; the remaining nine examples are likewise so, with detailed explanations provided at length.

Fifth, regarding the similarities and differences among the *siddhāntas*: other sutras also employ the four *siddhāntas* for purposes such as "shattering the three to reveal the one" and "shattering the traces to reveal the fundamental," yet they differ from this [text].
This constitutes two parts:
first, the Trace Gate (Ji-men) clarifies the difference;
second, the Origin Gate (Ben-men) clarifies the difference.

Regarding the differences in the Trace Gate (*jiamen*): within the Tripiṭaka, there is also the intent to use the four *siddhāntas* for the purpose of refuting and abolishing [false views], yet it is only for the sake of [attaining] *sa-upadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and *an-upadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, and so forth.

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (the *Dapin*), the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise employed with the intent of refuting, establishing, and setting aside according to the four *siddhāntas*; however, while one may awaken to the true principle, it is not yet fully perfected for long, and so forth.

Within the Vaipulya [sūtras], there is likewise the refutation of three [vehicles] to reveal the one; while there is partial agreement regarding bodhisattvas, those of the two vehicles cannot enter the reality. Thus, the ten disciples were rebuked by Vimalakīrti, falling into the eight heterodoxies and no longer being counted among the assembly—these are words of refutation and censure.
The inconceivable path of the Mahāyāna is praised by means of the four *siddhāntas*, yet those of the two vehicles do not awaken to it.

This sutra employs the four *siddhāntas* so that those of the two vehicles may sever their doubts, eliminate their attachments, enter the Buddha’s true path, and receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood.
Thus, one knows that this sutra employs the four *siddhāntas* with skillful artistry.
The text says:
"Its words and phrases are gentle and supple, delighting the hearts of all."
Śāriputra, having understood, said:

"The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, has skillfully explained this with parables; my mind is as calm as the ocean, and upon hearing this, the net of my doubts is severed... I abide now within true wisdom."
This is precisely the meaning [of the passage].
Question:
The Lotus Sūtra reveals the One Vehicle by relying on the prior refutations; without the preliminary ripening [of the faculties], one would not understand it even now.
Answer: That one attains awakening today is due to [criticism] leveled in the past; however, the merit belongs solely to this sutra, and the name does not belong to that [other teaching].

It is like a hundred people surrounding a single thief together: although the power of the siege actually relies on the multitude, it is only the one who captures the thief who receives the credit, and it does not belong to all a hundred people, and so forth.
This sutra reveals the provisional to manifest the real; its fourfold *siddhānta* efficacy is preeminently powerful and majestic, and so forth.
Its revelation of the origins to manifest the fundamental nature makes its fourfold *siddhānta* eternally distinct from all other sutras.
Why is this? As for the power and function within the traces, they have already appeared in various teachings;
yet among all the sutras, not a single one of the ten functions of the source exists, let alone all ten!
The *siddhānta* of the traces has already appeared in various sutras, whereas the *siddhānta* of the fundamental reality does not appear even once in any sutra, let alone in its fourfold form!
This can be inferred through reason; there is no need for extensive documentation.
